topStories.headline: Board of Supervisors Votes Unanimously to Extend Data Center Freeze Through September 2027
topStories.dek: The citywide moratorium on new data center construction was extended by ten months on November 17, with the Paul Avenue facility in Bayview at the center of the debate.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's Board of Supervisors voted unanimously on Tuesday, November 17, to extend the city's zoning moratorium on new data centers until September 2027, giving city planners ten months to study the environmental and infrastructure impacts of the facilities. The original 45-day pause was set to expire at the end of November, and the extension heads to Mayor Daniel Lurie's desk, where it takes effect in ten days unless he returns it — though any veto could be overridden by a four-fifths majority.

The vote has direct implications for Bayview-Hunters Point. The Paul Avenue corridor in the neighborhood already hosts NOVVA, an operating data center, and a proposed expansion of that facility would have been blocked by the moratorium. Outgoing District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton, who sponsored both the original pause and its extension, said before the vote that the city does not yet understand what data centers are doing to its communities.

The extension came one week after the city's Planning Department released a report warning that San Francisco's power grid is already near capacity — even before any new data centers come online. That finding gave additional weight to concerns raised by Bayview residents and community groups who have been monitoring the Paul Avenue campus for months. Supervisor-elect Theo Ellington, who will take over District 10 in January, had called for a data center moratorium specifically for southeast San Francisco during his campaign.

Data centers have become a flashpoint across the Bay Area. Oakland voted unanimously to extend its own moratorium through October 2027, and San Mateo County enacted a temporary ban on facilities in unincorporated areas the same week. The Planning Department has identified up to 15 potential data center sites in San Francisco, many of them downtown, though it acknowledges its inventory is not complete.

topStories.headline: Eighteen-Foot Burning Man Sculpture Lands at Bayview Gateway as New Source of Light
topStories.dek: "NewClear Neural," an LED-lit, interactive head by artist Ghazaleh Dasti, was installed at 2048 Cargo Way on November 12 as part of the Big Art Loop public art trail.
topStories.body:
A large sculptural head made of faceted purple metal panels and illuminated by shifting LED lights was installed at Bayview Gateway Park on Thursday, November 12. The piece, titled "NewClear Neural" and created by artist Ghazaleh Dasti, stands 18 feet tall and originally debuted at Burning Man in 2025. It is now the latest stop on the South City segment of Big Art Loop, a privately funded initiative placing temporary large-scale sculptures across a 34-mile citywide trail.

According to the Big Art Loop website, the sculpture is designed as an immersive human head whose lights trace neural pathways across its surface, responding to sounds picked up by embedded microphones — cars, voices, birdsong — and animating them as patterns of light. Visitors can step inside and operate a hand-powered carousel that generates electricity to run the piece.

The installation joins two other Big Art Loop works already in Bayview-Hunters Point: "Whispers of Waste" at India Basin and "Bloom" at Heron's Head Park. The sculpture is slated to remain at the Cargo Way site until November 2027, with a public celebration planned for early spring featuring Dasti and Bayview artist Malik Seneferu.

The T-Third Street Muni line, which runs along Third Street adjacent to the gateway, also got good news this week: the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency confirmed that overnight maintenance work on the line has concluded, restoring normal late-night service to the corridor.

topStories.headline: Theo Ellington Wins District 10 Supervisor Race in Decisive Victory
topStories.dek: The Bayview native and Ruth Williams Opera House director captured roughly 65 percent of the final ranked-choice vote to succeed outgoing Supervisor Shamann Walton.
topStories.body:
Theo Ellington declared victory in the race for San Francisco's District 10 supervisor seat on election night, November 3, and subsequent ballot counts confirmed the result. With almost all ballots counted as of November 10, Ellington held approximately 65 percent of the vote after ranked-choice tabulation, defeating a field of nine other candidates. His closest competitors were Dion-Jay Brookter and J.R. Eppler.

Ellington is a third-generation San Franciscan born and raised in Bayview-Hunters Point, and has served as executive director of the Ruth Williams Bayview Opera House. He previously worked as director of homelessness initiatives for The Salvation Army San Francisco and as public-affairs director for the Golden State Warriors, and has served on several city commissions.

District 10 covers the southeast corner of the city, including Bayview-Hunters Point, Potrero Hill, Visitacion Valley, and Candlestick Point — neighborhoods that Ellington said during the campaign deserve the same focus and resources as the rest of San Francisco. Among his stated priorities: independent verification of environmental testing at the Hunters Point Naval Shipyard before any land is transferred, and a data center moratorium for southeast San Francisco.

Outgoing Supervisor Walton, who has represented the district since 2018, called on the community to respect voters' choice and move forward. Mayor Daniel Lurie, who endorsed Ellington, made a surprise appearance at the election-night victory party. Ellington is expected to be sworn in in January 2027.

moreNews.headline: Gunshot Victim Found Near Visitacion Valley Middle School on November 13
moreNews.body: A deceased person with a gunshot wound to the head was discovered on the afternoon of Friday, November 13, at the 500 block of Raymond Avenue in Visitacion Valley, on the edge of John McLaren Park near Visitacion Valley Middle School. A Department of Public Works crew was cleaning in the area when workers found the body and a firearm and called police. As of the weekend, San Francisco police had not determined whether the wound was self-inflicted or whether foul play was involved, and the victim had not been publicly identified.
